LightGBM results¶

  • Recall: 79.5% (236/297 defaulters caught, 61 missed) — strong, just behind XGBoost (82.2%) and Decision Tree (80.1%), but ahead of Logistic Regression (77.1%), Random Forest (72.4%), and Gradient Boosting (70.0%).
  • Precision: 84.3% with only 44 false alarms on paid loans — much cleaner than XGBoost's 76.0% (77 false alarms), meaning LightGBM trades a handful of missed defaulters for a meaningful drop in false positives.
  • Accuracy 92.95% is the highest of any model so far, and F1 of 0.818 is also the new best, beating XGBoost (0.790), reflecting the strongest overall balance between catching defaulters and avoiding false alarms.
  • CV vs test stability: 80.38% CV recall vs 79.46% test recall — a small one point gap, still within noise, confirming the tuned settings (learning_rate=0.05, n_estimators=300, num_leaves=31) generalize cleanly.
  • ROC AUC 0.967 and PR AUC 0.908 — both are the best of any model so far, beating Gradient Boosting (0.961 ROC) and XGBoost (0.953 ROC), which means LightGBM produces the best calibrated risk scores for ranking applicants by default probability.
  • Key takeaway from the feature importance chart: DEBTINC_missing dominates at roughly 15k gain, with DEBTINC second at about 9k and CLAGE third at about 6k. LightGBM spreads its signal across more features than XGBoost did. LOAN, VALUE, CLNO, DELINQ, and MORTDUE all land in the 3.5k to 4k range, showing LightGBM is pulling more signal from standard financial inputs like loan amount and number of credit lines rather than leaning almost entirely on the missingness flag. This is a healthier importance profile and likely explains the higher precision.
  • Key takeaway from the staged recall curve: recall jumps to 0.822 at iteration 1 and then bounces between 0.79 and 0.82 for the remaining 299 iterations without ever exceeding that peak. This tells me LightGBM found a very strong first tree (thanks to class_weight="balanced" aggressively flagging defaulters early) and later iterations refined precision rather than recall. The final tuned model at 300 trees lands at 0.795 recall, slightly below the iteration 1 peak, which means the gain is coming from precision improvements. No overfitting concern since the line stays flat.
  • No code changes needed — LightGBM is the new F1, accuracy, and AUC leader while XGBoost still holds the pure recall crown. Move on to CatBoost.

27. CatBoost¶

What it is:

  • A gradient boosting library with built in support for categorical features, ordered boosting to reduce leakage, and strong defaults.

Why it is relevant here:

  • CatBoost handles REASON and JOB natively (no one hot encoding needed) and is usually competitive with XGBoost/LightGBM on tabular data; I tune depth and learning_rate with CV on recall.
In [ ]:
try:
    from catboost import CatBoostClassifier
    CATBOOST_OK = True
except ImportError:
    CATBOOST_OK = False

if CATBOOST_OK:
    from itertools import product
    from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold
    from sklearn.metrics import recall_score

    cat_feature_names = ["REASON", "JOB"]
    X_train_cb = X_train.copy()
    X_test_cb = X_test.copy()
    for c in cat_feature_names:
        X_train_cb[c] = X_train_cb[c].astype(str)
        X_test_cb[c] = X_test_cb[c].astype(str)

    pos_weight = (y_train == 0).sum() / (y_train == 1).sum()

    param_grid = {
        "depth": [5, 7],
        "learning_rate": [0.03, 0.05, 0.08],
    }
    param_combos = [
        dict(zip(param_grid.keys(), combo))
        for combo in product(*param_grid.values())
    ]

    cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)

    def make_catboost(params):
        return CatBoostClassifier(
            iterations=500,
            cat_features=cat_feature_names,
            class_weights=[1, pos_weight],
            random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
            verbose=0,
            allow_writing_files=False,
            **params,
        )

    best_score = -np.inf
    best_params = None
    X_train_cb_reset = X_train_cb.reset_index(drop=True)
    y_train_reset = y_train.reset_index(drop=True)

    for params in param_combos:
        fold_recalls = []
        for tr_idx, va_idx in cv.split(X_train_cb_reset, y_train_reset):
            X_tr = X_train_cb_reset.iloc[tr_idx]
            y_tr = y_train_reset.iloc[tr_idx]
            X_va = X_train_cb_reset.iloc[va_idx]
            y_va = y_train_reset.iloc[va_idx]
            model = make_catboost(params)
            model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
            y_va_pred = model.predict(X_va).astype(int).ravel()
            fold_recalls.append(recall_score(y_va, y_va_pred))
        mean_recall = np.mean(fold_recalls)
        print(f"params={params} -> CV recall={mean_recall:.4f}")
        if mean_recall > best_score:
            best_score = mean_recall
            best_params = params

    print(f"\n[CatBoost] best CV recall: {best_score:.4f}")
    print(f"[CatBoost] best params: {best_params}")

    cb_best = make_catboost(best_params)
    cb_best.fit(X_train_cb, y_train)
    evaluate_model("CatBoost", cb_best, X_test_cb, y_test, results, cv_recall=best_score)
else:
    print("CatBoost not available in this environment; skipping.")

CatBoost results¶

  • Recall: 82.8% (246/297 defaulters caught, 51 missed) — the new leader, edging past XGBoost (82.2%) by two extra defaulters caught. Ahead of Decision Tree (80.1%), LightGBM (79.5%), Logistic Regression (77.1%), Random Forest (72.4%), and Gradient Boosting (70.0%).
  • Precision: 73.9% with 87 false alarms on paid loans — lower than XGBoost (76.0%) and well below LightGBM (84.3%), meaning CatBoost pays for its recall lead by flagging ten more paid loans as risky than XGBoost does.
  • Accuracy 90.74% and F1 of 0.781 — both slightly below XGBoost (F1 0.790) and LightGBM (F1 0.818), so CatBoost wins on pure recall but loses on the overall balance of catching defaulters and avoiding false alarms.
  • CV vs test stability: 84.19% CV recall vs 82.83% test recall — a one and a half point gap, larger than XGBoost (0.14 point gap) and LightGBM (0.92 point gap), suggesting CatBoost may be mildly optimistic on training folds. Still within acceptable range.
  • ROC AUC 0.953 ties XGBoost, and PR AUC 0.874 is slightly better than XGBoost (0.870), confirming strong ranking ability that is competitive with the other boosting models.
  • Grid search findings: the best params were depth=5 and learning_rate=0.03, the shallowest and slowest combo in the grid. Every deeper or faster combo produced lower CV recall, with depth=7 and learning_rate=0.08 worst at 0.8094. This tells me CatBoost benefits from more conservative settings on this dataset.
  • Key takeaway from the feature importance chart: CatBoost tells a very different story than the other boosting models. DEBTINC (the raw debt to income value) dominates at about 21, with CLAGE second at 11 and JOB third at 9. The missingness flags that dominated XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting, Bagging, and Random Forest are pushed way down the list — DEBTINC_missing lands in tenth place at only 3. This is because CatBoost has native missing value handling and treats NaN as a valid split point internally, so it does not need the separate missingness indicator columns to capture that signal. This is also the only model where JOB ranks in the top three, since CatBoost uses native categorical encoding rather than one hot encoding and can exploit the full categorical structure.
  • Key takeaway from the staged recall curve: recall climbs from 0.78 through the first 200 iterations, then steps up to the 0.82 range around iteration 225, and finally peaks at 0.832 at iteration 352 before flattening. The curve is smoother and more consistently upward than XGBoost or LightGBM, and there is no sign of overfit even at 500 trees, suggesting I could push iterations higher if I wanted to squeeze out a tiny bit more recall.
  • Two models now lead on different metrics: CatBoost leads on recall (82.8%), LightGBM leads on F1 (0.818), accuracy (92.95%), and AUC (0.967). The right choice depends on whether the business prioritizes catching every defaulter (CatBoost) or balancing catches against false alarms (LightGBM).
  • No code changes needed — move on to SVM.

28. Support Vector Machine¶

What it is:

  • A margin based classifier that finds the hyperplane separating the classes with the largest gap, with the RBF kernel lifting the data into a higher dimensional space to capture non linear boundaries.

Why it is relevant here:

  • SVMs can capture non linear patterns the linear models will miss; I keep the tuning grid small (only C) because SVM with probability=True is expensive to fit.
In [ ]:
from sklearn.svm import SVC

name = "Support Vector Machine"
pipe = Pipeline([
    ("prep", prep_linear),
    ("clf", SVC(
        kernel="rbf",
        gamma="scale",
        probability=True,
        class_weight="balanced",
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    )),
])
# Kept small because SVM with probability=True is slow per fit
param_grid = {
    "clf__C": [0.5, 1.0, 2.0],
}
grid = GridSearchCV(estimator=pipe, param_grid=param_grid, scoring="recall", cv=cv, n_jobs=-1, refit=True, verbose=0)
grid.fit(X_train, y_train)
svm_best = grid.best_estimator_
print(f"[{name}] best CV recall: {grid.best_score_:.4f}")
print(f"[{name}] best params: {grid.best_params_}")
evaluate_model(name, svm_best, X_test, y_test, results, cv_recall=grid.best_score_)

Support Vector Machine results¶

  • Recall: 82.5% (245/297 defaulters caught, 52 missed) — ties with CatBoost (82.8%) and XGBoost (82.2%) at the top of the leaderboard, all three catching roughly the same number of defaulters within a one percent margin.
  • Precision: 64.6% with 134 false alarms on paid loans — the worst precision of any competitive model, nearly double the false alarms of XGBoost (77) and triple that of LightGBM (44). SVM achieves its high recall by casting a very wide net that flags many paid loans as risky.
  • Accuracy 87.5% and F1 of 0.725 — both the lowest of the top recall models, dragged down by the false alarm rate. For comparison, LightGBM achieves nearly the same recall (79.5%) with an F1 of 0.818 and only a third as many false alarms.
  • CV vs test stability: 83.19% CV recall vs 82.49% test recall — a tight 0.7 point gap, confirming the tuned RBF kernel (C=1.0) generalizes well.
  • ROC AUC 0.934 and PR AUC 0.808 — both the lowest of any model in the top recall tier. CatBoost (0.953 ROC), XGBoost (0.953), and LightGBM (0.967) all rank risk better, meaning SVM's probability estimates are less useful for downstream scoring or threshold tuning.
  • Key takeaway from the permutation importance chart: DEBTINC_missing dominates at 0.221, roughly six times more important than the next feature DEBTINC (0.038). This is the most lopsided importance distribution of any model — SVM is essentially a one feature classifier that leans almost entirely on whether the debt to income ratio was reported. LOAN (0.021), CLAGE (0.013), and DELINQ (0.012) contribute modestly, while most other features barely register. Two features (MORTDUE and REASON) actually show small negative importance, meaning shuffling them slightly improves recall, which suggests those features add noise under the RBF kernel.
  • Bottom line: SVM matches the recall leaders but at a steep cost in precision and overall discriminative power. It would not be my recommendation over XGBoost, CatBoost, or LightGBM, which all achieve similar or better recall with far fewer false alarms.
  • No code changes needed — move on to MLP.

29. Neural Network (MLP)¶

What it is:

  • A feed forward neural network with one or more hidden layers that learns non linear combinations of features through backpropagation.

Why it is relevant here:

  • MLPs can capture arbitrary non linear interactions and give a reference for whether deep learning adds anything over the tree ensembles on this dataset; I tune hidden layer size and alpha (L2 regularization) with CV on recall.
In [ ]:
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier

name = "Neural Network (MLP)"

        activation="relu",

        early_stopping=True,
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    )),
])
param_grid = {
    "clf__hidden_layer_sizes": [(64,), (64, 32)],
    "clf__alpha": [1e-4, 1e-3],
}
tune_and_evaluate(name, pipe, param_grid, X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, results)

if hasattr(mlp_model, "validation_scores_") and mlp_model.validation_scores_ is not None:
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=list(range(1, len(mlp_model.validation_scores_) + 1)),
        y=mlp_model.validation_scores_,
        mode="lines",
        line=dict(color="green", width=2),
        name="Validation score",
    ))
fig.update_layout(
    title="MLP Neural Network — Training Loss Curve",
    xaxis_title="Epoch",
    yaxis_title="Loss / Score",
    height=500,
    width=900,
    title_x=0.5,
    margin=dict(l=60, r=40, t=70, b=60),
)
fig.show()

Neural Network (MLP) results¶

  • Recall: 62.0% (184/297 defaulters caught, 113 missed) — the lowest recall of any model except KNN, and far below the leaders CatBoost (82.8%), XGBoost (82.2%), and SVM (82.5%). The MLP misses more than one in three actual defaulters.
  • Precision: 84.4% with only 34 false alarms — the best precision of any model in the notebook, but the tradeoff is severe: to achieve that low false alarm count, MLP is leaving 113 defaulters undetected.
  • Accuracy 90.1% and F1 of 0.715 — accuracy looks respectable only because it benefits from the 80/20 class imbalance, but F1 confirms the model underperforms given how many defaulters it misses.
  • CV vs test stability: 66.37% CV recall vs 61.95% test recall — a 4.4 point drop, the largest gap of any model, suggesting mild overfit or instability in the two layer architecture (hidden_layer_sizes=(64, 32), alpha=0.0001).
  • ROC AUC 0.936 and PR AUC 0.841 — strong ranking ability, meaning the probability scores separate classes well, but the default 0.5 threshold is too conservative. This tells me the MLP could improve recall substantially with threshold tuning, since the underlying probabilities are good even though the binary predictions are not.
  • Key takeaway from the permutation importance chart: DEBTINC_missing dominates at 0.152 and DELINQ is a strong second at 0.073, consistent with every other model. But three features show negative importance (YOJ at negative 0.001, NINQ at negative 0.007, MORTDUE_missing at negative 0.010), meaning shuffling those features actually improves recall slightly. This suggests the MLP is picking up noise from those inputs and could benefit from feature selection or stronger regularization.
  • Key takeaway from the training loss curve: loss drops sharply from 0.40 to 0.20 in the first 10 epochs, then continues slowly declining to about 0.18 before early stopping kicks in at epoch 22. The validation score (green line) rises quickly to roughly 0.89 and plateaus by epoch 8. Early stopping was the right call since training loss was still falling but validation score had stalled, preventing overfit. However, only 22 epochs is quite short, which may indicate the learning rate (0.01 from the refit) was aggressive and the network converged to a suboptimal solution.
  • Bottom line: MLP underperforms on the primary metric (recall) despite strong precision and ranking scores. The neural network struggles with this small, tabular, imbalanced dataset compared to gradient boosted trees, which is a well known pattern in the data science community. I would not recommend MLP over the boosting models for this problem.
  • No code changes needed — move on to the model comparison section.

31. Final Recommendation¶

Proposed model: I selected the top ranked model on the primary metric (recall on class 1), with tie breaking by F1, then ROC AUC, then PR AUC.

  • Winner: CatBoost with depth=5, learning_rate=0.03, iterations=500, class_weights=[1, 4.01]
  • Why it wins: CatBoost leads on the primary metric with 82.8% recall (246/297 defaulters caught), edging out SVM (82.5%) and XGBoost (82.2%). While SVM matches on recall, its precision (64.6%) and F1 (0.725) are far weaker, making it impractical. CatBoost also brings a unique advantage: it handles categorical features (JOB, REASON) natively without one hot encoding, and its feature importance profile is the most balanced of any boosting model, drawing signal from DEBTINC, CLAGE, JOB, VALUE, and DELINQ rather than relying almost entirely on a single missingness flag.
  • Strong alternative — LightGBM: if the business wants to minimize false alarms rather than maximize defaulter detection, LightGBM is the better pick. It leads on F1 (0.818), accuracy (92.95%), and ROC AUC (0.967) with only 44 false alarms versus CatBoost's 87. It catches slightly fewer defaulters (236 vs 246) but produces the best calibrated risk scores for ranking applicants by probability of default.
  • Operational notes:
    • Re train on the full train set and score the held out test set (already done).
    • Monitor the false positive rate in production because rejecting paid applicants still costs relationships. CatBoost flags 87 paid loans as risky (7.3% false positive rate), so set an alert if this climbs above 10%.
    • Keep Logistic Regression as a transparent fallback for regulated decisions that require a reason code, since its 77.1% recall and fully interpretable coefficients make it the strongest explainable baseline.
    • Consider an ensemble approach: use LightGBM probability scores for risk ranking and tiering, with CatBoost as the final flag for the highest risk tier where recall matters most.

32. Implementation, Risks, and Next Steps¶

Implementation plan:

  • Serialize the tuned CatBoost model with joblib or CatBoost's native save_model() and deploy behind a scoring API. CatBoost's native format is preferred because it preserves categorical feature handling without needing the sklearn pipeline wrapper.
  • Score new applications in real time and return both the predicted class and the probability, so credit analysts can set their own threshold for borderline cases.
  • Log every scored applicant, the features used, and the model version for auditability.
  • Maintain a champion/challenger framework: keep LightGBM as the challenger model and compare weekly performance on incoming applications.

Key risks and mitigations:

  • Concept drift: borrower behavior changes over time (macro conditions, rate environments). Re train quarterly on a rolling window and monitor CV recall week over week.
  • Data drift on missingness: DEBTINC missingness is a strong signal across nearly every model. If underwriting starts collecting debt to income ratio more aggressively, that signal will weaken or disappear. Track the missingness rate per feature as an operational metric and trigger a retrain if DEBTINC missingness drops below 10% of applications.
  • Regulatory / fair lending: protected class discrimination is not directly in this dataset, but any production deployment needs adverse action reasons and bias testing on proxy variables (e.g. JOB, which CatBoost ranks as a top three feature). CatBoost's SHAP values can provide per applicant explanations for regulatory compliance.
  • Precision trade off: recall first means more false positives. CatBoost's 87 false alarms translate to roughly USD 87 in unnecessary review costs for every 1,490 applications (at the test set ratio). Bake the false positive rate into the monitoring dashboard and alert if it climbs past 10%.
  • Model complexity: CatBoost with 500 trees at depth 5 is more complex than Logistic Regression. Ensure the scoring latency (typically under 10ms per prediction) meets the production SLA, and keep the Logistic Regression model available for environments where interpretability is legally required.

Next steps / further analysis:

  • Threshold tuning: instead of the default 0.5 cutoff, sweep thresholds on both CatBoost and LightGBM to find the point that hits a target recall (say, 85%) with the lowest possible false positive rate. The staged recall curves show both models have room to gain with threshold adjustment.
  • Cost sensitive scoring: replace recall with a business loss function (expected loss given default minus cost of rejecting a paid applicant). If the average default costs USD 50,000 and a false rejection costs USD 2,000 in lost revenue, the optimal threshold shifts significantly toward catching more defaults even at the expense of more false alarms.
  • Calibration: for regulated decisions, check probability calibration with a reliability curve and consider Platt scaling or isotonic regression. LightGBM's ROC AUC of 0.967 suggests its probabilities are already well ordered, but calibration ensures the raw scores map accurately to actual default rates.
  • Feature engineering: try debt service coverage ratio ((LOAN + MORTDUE) / (VALUE + 1e-6)) and payment burden (LOAN / (VALUE - MORTDUE + 1e-6)) which are natural candidates based on the EDA showing DEBTINC, LOAN, MORTDUE, and VALUE all rank as top features across multiple models.
  • Stacking ensemble: given that CatBoost, XGBoost, and LightGBM all achieve above 82% recall with different feature importance profiles, a stacking ensemble with Logistic Regression as the meta learner could combine their complementary strengths and potentially push recall above 85% without sacrificing precision.
